Time-series data is all around us—from air quality measurements to financial market trends. In this project, we explore advanced temporal data analysis techniques using Python’s Pandas library along with other powerful tools such as Statsmodels and Matplotlib. Our goal is to transform raw air quality data into actionable insights by extracting time features, aggregating trends, computing rolling statistics, performing seasonal decomposition, and even generating basic forecasts using a naive method.

Whether you’re a data scientist, analyst, or enthusiast interested in learning advanced time-series techniques, this guide will help you understand each step of the data analysis pipeline.

Project Overview

In this project, we utilize an air quality dataset (in our example, an Excel file) that contains readings for different pollutants along with their timestamps. We will:

  • Extract temporal features such as year, month, day of the week, and hour from the datetime index.
  • Aggregate pollutant levels by day of the week to understand periodic behavior.
  • Apply rolling statistics to smooth out noise and reveal trends.
  • Decompose the time series into its trend, seasonal, and residual components using an additive model.
  • Generate a naive forecast by replicating the last observed value for a set number of future time steps.

These techniques enable you to perform in-depth temporal analysis and basic forecasting, laying the foundation for more advanced forecasting techniques later on.

Dataset and Initial Setup

We begin by loading the air quality dataset from an Excel file. The dataset is expected to have a datetime column that we parse and set as the DataFrame index. This makes it easier to conduct time-series operations like resampling and feature extraction. Additionally, redundant columns (such as location details that may not contribute to the temporal analysis) are dropped.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from pandas import DataFrame
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import seasonal_decompose
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Load the Air Quality dataset (example from an Excel file)
file_path = "air_quality_long_edited.xlsx"
df = pd.read_excel(file_path, parse_dates=["datetime"], index_col="datetime")

Note: Parsing dates and setting the datetime column as the index is fundamental for time-series operations. For more details, see the Pandas Time Series documentation.

Temporal Feature Extraction

Once the data is loaded, the first step is extracting temporal features. This function adds new columns for:

  • Year – Useful for long-term trends.
  • Month – Affects seasonal variation.
  • Day of Week – Offers insights into periodic behavior such as weekday versus weekend.
  • Hour – Crucial for intraday patterns.
def extract_temporal_features(df: DataFrame):
    df["year"] = df.index.year
    df["month"] = df.index.month
    df["day_of_week"] = df.index.day_name()
    df["hour"] = df.index.hour
    return df

# Apply temporal feature extraction
df = extract_temporal_features(df)

Why extract temporal features?
Adding these features allows us to analyze how pollutant levels vary with time at multiple granularities. It is especially useful when seasonal patterns or recurrent cycles might influence the data.

Aggregating Data by Day of the Week

To understand how pollutant levels vary throughout the week, we aggregate data by the day of the week. This function filters the DataFrame for a specified pollutant and calculates the mean value for each weekday.

def aggregate_by_day_of_week(df: DataFrame, pollutant=None):
    aggr = df[df["parameter"].str.lower() == pollutant.lower()]
    result = aggr.groupby("day_of_week")["value"].mean().sort_index()
    print(f"aggregate_by_day_of_week: {result}")
    return result

For example, aggregating NO₂ (if specified) can reveal whether there are significant differences between weekdays and weekends. This step is a powerful way to visualize periodic trends that might be driven by human activity, weather, or other factors.

Rolling Statistics

Rolling (or moving) averages help in smoothing out short-term fluctuations and highlighting longer-term trends or cycles in time-series data. The function below computes a rolling mean for the value column over a user-specified window (e.g., 7 days).

def apply_rolling_mean(df: DataFrame, window):
    df[f"value_RollingMean_{window}"] = df["value"].rolling(window=window).mean()
    return df

Usage Tip:
The window size (e.g., 7 days) can be adjusted depending on the frequency and variability of the data. This technique is particularly useful in identifying trends that are obscured by the noise inherent in raw data.

Seasonal Decomposition

Seasonal decomposition splits a time series into three components: trend, seasonal, and residual (noise). This technique is invaluable for understanding the underlying patterns within the data. We use the seasonal_decompose function from Statsmodels with an additive model.

def decompose_time_series(df: DataFrame, column, freq):
    decomposition = seasonal_decompose(df[column].dropna(), model='additive', period=freq)
    decomposition.plot()
    plt.show()
    return decomposition.trend, decomposition.seasonal, decomposition.resid

In this context, freq=365 might be used for annual seasonality if the data supports such a cycle. The resulting plots give you a clear view of how trends and seasonal components evolve over time.

Reference:
For additional details, see the Statsmodels Seasonal Decompose documentation.

Naive Forecasting

A naive forecast is one of the simplest forecasting methods. It predicts that the future value will be the same as the last observed value. Although rudimentary, naive forecasts can serve as a baseline for comparison with more complex forecasting models.

def naive_forecast(df: DataFrame, column, steps):
    forecast: list = [df[column].iloc[-1]] * steps
    print(forecast)
    return forecast

This function simply replicates the most recent value for the specified number of steps ahead.

Generating the Full Report

The generate_report function ties all the previous functions together. It:

  1. Aggregates NO₂ by day of the week.
  2. Applies a rolling mean with a window of 7.
  3. Decomposes the time series to examine trend, seasonal, and residual components.
  4. Produces a naive forecast for the next 7 time steps.
def generate_report(df: DataFrame):

    # Step 2: Aggregate NO2 by Day of the Week
    weekly_avg = aggregate_by_day_of_week(df, "no2")
    print("Weekly Average NO2 Concentrations:")
    print(weekly_avg)

    # Step 3: Apply Rolling Mean
    df = apply_rolling_mean(df, window=7)
    print("Rolling Mean applied. Sample data:")
    print(df.head(10))

    # Step 4: Decompose Time Series
    print("Decomposing the time series...")
    trend, seasonal, resid = decompose_time_series(df, "value", freq=365)
    print("Trend Sample:")
    print(trend.head())

    # Step 5: Naive Forecast
    print("Naive Forecast for 7 steps ahead:")
    forecast = naive_forecast(df, "parameter", steps=7)
    print(forecast)

This orchestrated report gives you an end-to-end view of the temporal structure and forecasting potential of your air quality data.

Conclusion

This project demonstrates advanced techniques for temporal data analysis and forecasting using Pandas and complementary Python libraries. By extracting time features, aggregating data by weekday, applying rolling statistics, and performing seasonal decomposition, you gain a comprehensive view of the temporal structure within your dataset. The naive forecasting component provides a simple baseline, which you can later enhance with more sophisticated models.

With these tools in your arsenal, you're now well-equipped to dive into more advanced forecasting and time-series analysis projects. Experiment, extend, and explore further—happy coding and data exploring!

This extensive tutorial is designed to provide deep insights into advanced temporal data analysis. Enjoy applying these techniques to your own projects and learning more about the fascinating world of time-series forecasting!
